headline: Medium pairwise risk: shared-bus Pipecat can feed RD-Agent’s browser/API workflows, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Pipecat’s shared bus and stdin/stdout make its outputs easy to bridge into RD-Agent, which runs browsers and consumes external content. That creates a plausible instruction-hijack path if Pipecat relays untrusted text and RD-Agent treats it as agent input. The interaction is inferred from docs, not directly observed, so uncertainty pushes to medium.
conditions: IF Pipecat output is forwarded into RD-Agent prompts or browser tasks without sanitization, injection is possible.
IF both agents share a bus or message queue carrying untrusted text, attacker instructions can traverse the pair.
mitigations: Add a strict content separator and strip imperative language before handoff.
Route Pipecat output through a human review step for browser-driving tasks.
Disable automatic prompt chaining between the agents.
Log and flag any handoff containing URLs, code blocks, or instructions.
requires-engineering: implement provenance tags on shared-bus messages.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Pipecat touches audio, video, images, text, and conversation state, while RD-Agent handles papers, financial reports, execution traces, and logs. Pipecat’s allowlisted egress and RD-Agent’s broad egress/API use mean sensitive content can flow out of the pair in default-style workflows. The shared-bus model increases accidental cross-exposure risk.
conditions: IF Pipecat receives sensitive conversation/audio content and forwards it onto the shared bus, RD-Agent may ingest it.
IF RD-Agent processes those inputs with external APIs or browser sessions, the data can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Minimize shared-bus payloads to redacted summaries.
Block secrets, transcripts, and attachments from cross-agent transfer.
Use separate credentials and API keys per agent.
Turn off browser/API access for tasks that do not need external retrieval.
requires-engineering: add DLP filters on the bus.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Pipecat supports multiple instances on a shared bus, and RD-Agent also supports multiple instances with Docker-based isolation. Both have network egress and external API use, so overlapping writes are less about filesystem and more about shared mutable resources and concurrent outbound actions. The profiles do not prove locking, so the safer choice is medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same shared bus topic or shared external API quota, race conditions can occur.
IF either agent mutates shared files or logs without locking, concurrent corruption is possible.
mitigations: Assign separate bus topics or queues per agent.
Use per-agent API keys and quotas.
Serialize writes to any shared workspace.
Add a simple lock file around shared mutable resources.
requires-engineering: enforce optimistic concurrency checks on shared state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Pipecat can emit conversation state and external content, and RD-Agent is a research automation agent that can act through browsers and APIs. If RD-Agent treats Pipecat output as authoritative, a bad transcript or hallucinated fact can cascade into downstream actions or reports. Because the pair’s default workflow can chain outputs into actions, the blast radius is high.
conditions: IF RD-Agent consumes Pipecat output without verification, errors can propagate into research artifacts or browser actions.
IF Pipecat relays unverified external content, RD-Agent may act on false premises.
mitigations: Require a verification step before RD-Agent acts on Pipecat output.
Mark Pipecat-originated content as untrusted in prompts.
Limit RD-Agent to read-only retrieval for chained tasks.
Add citation checks before any report generation.
requires-engineering: implement confidence gating on handoffs.

E_compliance.rationale: Pipecat touches audio/video/text conversation state, while RD-Agent handles financial reports, competition datasets, and logs with API keys and Kaggle credentials. That combination creates a plausible retention and residency mismatch if regulated or sensitive data is routed from one to the other. The profiles do not document matching compliance controls, so medium is the prudent level.
conditions: IF EU PII, PHI, or regulated research data is routed through both agents, residency and retention obligations may diverge.
IF either agent logs or retains shared content longer than the other, deletion/export obligations can fail.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workflow.
Separate logs by data class and retention period.
Review API destinations before enabling the pair.
Purge shared transcripts after task completion.
requires-engineering: add policy-based retention controls.
